originalGroup.material:
The song next door

Someone next door practised the same piano tune every afternoon, but the music always ____1____ before the end. I wondered whether the player had forgotten the final notes.

I asked our neighbour Mr Bell about it. He laughed and said his grandson was learning it. The boy knew the whole song, but found one part ____2____. 

The next afternoon, I heard the music again. I noticed he did not always return to the ____3____. Sometimes he began in the middle and played only four notes. Then he tried them again, more slowly.

A week later, Mr Bell invited us to tea. His grandson played the tune for us. I knew every part, but hearing them all ____4____ felt new. We clapped after the quiet final note.

The boy asked if I wanted to learn the first line. I sat at the piano and immediately pressed the wrong ____5____. He showed me, then waited. I did not need him to play the whole song for me. I needed time to find those four notes ____6____.

 The next day, the piano next door began a ____7____ tune. I smiled at the sound of its unfinished phrases. This time I could imagine the ____8____ behind them. A whole performance might last two minutes, but learning it took ____9____. The pauses in the music were not empty afternoons. They were part of getting ____10____.

originalGroup.material:
The wheel on the basket

Grandma usually carried a basket to the market. When she hurt her arm, Dad bought her a small bag with ____1____. She could pull it along instead of carrying everything home.

I offered to pull it on our first trip. After we bought potatoes and apples, it felt much ____2____. Grandma checked it.

One wheel had a small stone beside it. She took the bag off the busy path and removed the stone. The wheel began to turn ____3____ again. Weight had not been the only problem.

We put a loaf above the apples. I wanted to add our potatoes there too, but Grandma showed me the bread. It was ____4____. Heavy potatoes could squash it. We placed them in the lower part instead.

Then it began to rain. Grandma pulled a cover over the bag and took her umbrella. I held the umbrella while she fastened the cover. We each had a ____5____, and neither of us had to do everything at once.

At home, we unpacked the food on the kitchen table. The loaf still had its round shape. Grandma checked what we had ____6____. I checked each item. We had everything except tea.

Dad would buy tea after work, so we did not need another ____7____. I put the empty bag away. I had thought helping meant taking the handle and doing the ____8____ alone. It had actually meant watching, asking and ____9____ small jobs. The bag made shopping easier, but it did not do the thinking for ____10____.

The road drawn in chalk

We drew a chalk town on the playground. There was a library, a hospital and a long ____1____ between them. We would act as townspeople.

I drew the library entrance on the wrong side. The road led to a blank wall. I added a short path to the door instead of ____2____ the whole building.

When the activity began, I became the librarian. Two visitors asked for books, so I pointed to a chalk ____3____ and invited them to imagine its books. 

Then rain began to fall. The teacher moved everyone inside. Through the window, we watched the bright lines become ____4____. Chalk in rain would not last.

Our teacher had taken photographs before the rain. She showed them on the classroom screen, and we described our different ____5____. The picture did not record our conversations.

I wrote a short note about the two visitors to my library. Another student described an imaginary bus journey. We put the notes ____6____ the photographs on a board. 

The next sunny week, we used a different part of the playground. This time, we drew the roads ____7____, before adding the buildings. We also left space for a park. It did not need to ____8____ the first one exactly. We could still make ____9____ choices. I gave my new library two doors. Nobody would have to walk through a wall to ____10____ a book.

The visitor at ten

Dad told me our cousin would arrive at ten on Saturday. I prepared a card and biscuits. At half past nine, I sat by the window to ____1____ for him.

A red car stopped outside. It was our neighbour returning Dad’s umbrella. The car was the right colour, but the visitor was the wrong ____2____.

At ten, nobody came.  Dad looked at his phone. Our cousin had sent a message: the bus was delayed, and he would arrive thirty minutes ____3____.

I could hear the bell from the kitchen. Dad suggested finishing my model ship there. I moved the model there and began fixing its paper ____4____. 

The bell rang at half past ten. This time it really was our cousin. He carried a small ____5____. Inside was a book about ships.

I showed him my model, with its last sail still loose. We finished it together before eating. He had arrived later than ____6____, but he had not missed the whole morning.

After lunch, we read his book. We compared a larger ship with my model. We compared the sails and drew a ____7____ for another one. 

When our cousin left, I found the first message on Dad's phone. The time had been a ____8____, not a promise that nothing could change. I still liked having things ready, but next time I would leave room for an ____9____. I would also check before shouting "Welcome!" to every red ____10____.
